title: Sell Mineral Rights in Powder River County, MT
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Powder River County, MT
metaDescription: Powder River County is the actual Powder River Basin, but the thinner Montana edge of it. I buy CBM and fee mineral interests here based on real production.
heroLead: This is the county the whole basin is named for, and it's also honestly the thinner northern edge of it.
intro: Powder River County sits at the top of the Powder River Basin, the same coal-seam gas trend that made Campbell County, Wyoming one of the most heavily developed CBM areas in the country. The Montana side never matched that density. Wyodak and Anderson coal-seam gas leasing reached into this county during the 2000s CBM boom, and some units are still producing, but well spacing here has generally been wider and development more selective than across the state line. If your family's interest is in Powder River County, I want you to understand that comparison honestly before we ever discuss a number.

Almost all the land in this county is fee land — there's no reservation trust status to navigate here, unlike Big Horn or Rosebud County to the north. That simplifies the process considerably, even though the underlying activity picture is more modest.

sections.heading: Why the Montana side of the Powder River Basin is thinner
paragraphs: Coal seam thickness, depth, and water handling economics all shift as you move north from the Wyoming core into Montana, and operators followed that economics — concentrating drilling where the coal was thickest and cheapest to produce. Powder River County saw real leasing and real wells, but nothing close to the saturation seen in Campbell County. I evaluate an interest here against that honest baseline.

sections.heading: What a lapsed CBM lease looks like here
paragraphs: A lot of 2000s-era CBM leasing in this county had short terms, and when gas prices fell in the following decade, plenty of acreage reverted to the mineral owner unleased. If your family hasn't seen a payment in years, that's consistent with a lapsed lease rather than mismanagement, and I check the recorded status before saying anything about value.

sections.heading: Ranch-family ownership and Broadus records
paragraphs: Powder River County is ranch country, and a lot of mineral interests here trace to homestead-era severances kept separate when a ranch was sold or passed down through a family. I pull the recorded chain from the Powder River County Clerk and Recorder in Broadus before I make any offer, confirming exactly who holds what share.

sections.heading: How I price interests on the thin edge of a named basin
paragraphs: I look at whether the parcel sits inside a still-active CBM spacing unit, on lapsed leasehold, or on ground that was never leased at all. Each of those is a genuinely different asset, and I won't collapse them into one number just because they all sit inside the county the basin is named for.

sections.heading: Water disposal and why it shaped this county's development
paragraphs: Coalbed methane production requires pulling large volumes of water out of the coal seam to release the gas, and handling that water was expensive here, more so than in parts of the Wyoming core with better disposal options nearby. That economic reality, as much as the geology itself, is why Powder River County never saw the well density its southern neighbor did. It's worth understanding if you're trying to make sense of why some units near your family's parcel were drilled and others, on paper similar ground, never were.

sections.heading: Broadus courthouse realities for older ranch families
paragraphs: A lot of the families I work with in this county have deep roots going back three or four generations on the same ranch, with mineral rights that were carved off in a sale decades ago and largely forgotten since. The Broadus courthouse holds that whole history, and I go through it methodically rather than asking a family to reconstruct decades of paperwork themselves.

faqs.question: Is Powder River County as active as the Wyoming side of the basin?
faqs.answer: No, and I say that plainly. Development here has always been thinner and more selective than the Campbell County, Wyoming core.

faqs.question: Is my mineral interest trust land or fee land?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly fee land — there's no reservation trust status in this county, which simplifies the sale process.

faqs.question: Our CBM lease hasn't paid anything in years — is it still active?
faqs.answer: Possibly not. A lot of 2000s-era leases here had short terms and lapsed when gas prices fell. I check the recorded status before quoting.

faqs.question: How do you verify ownership in this county?
faqs.answer: Through the recorded deed chain at the Powder River County Clerk and Recorder in Broadus, the same as any ranch-country parcel in eastern Montana.

faqs.question: Is a never-leased interest here worth anything?
faqs.answer: Often yes, priced as long-term potential rather than current income. I explain that distinction clearly before making an offer.

faqs.question: Why did some units in the county get drilled and neighboring ones didn't?
faqs.answer: Largely water disposal economics. CBM production requires handling significant water volumes, and that cost was higher here than in parts of the Wyoming core, which made operators more selective.

faqs.question: My family's mineral rights were carved off a ranch sale decades ago — can you still trace that?
faqs.answer: Yes. I work through the Broadus courthouse records methodically to reconstruct that history rather than asking you to piece it together yourself.
